dataset.name: Gap-filled methane and carbon dioxide fluxes across two ecosystem states at the US-OWC AmeriFlux site (2015−2016, 2020−2022)
description: This dataset contains gap-filled measurements of methane flux (FCH4), net ecosystem CO2 exchange (NEE) partitioned into gross primary productivity (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (RE), as well as latent heat flux (LE) from a Great Lakes coastal freshwater wetland at the US-OWC AmeriFlux site. The dataset covers the peak growing seasons (June−September) of 2015−2016, dominated by Typha spp., and 2020−2022, characterized by floating-leaved species (lotus and water lily). These data were generated to investigate how rising water levels and vegetation shifts influence CH4 and CO2 fluxes across two distinct ecosystem states in this wetland.

The dataset, provided in CSV format, includes half-hourly gap-filled flux data from June to September for 2015, 2016, 2020, 2021, and 2022. The gap-filled data refers to measurements where missing values due to instrument issues or quality control were filled using artificial neural networks (ANNs).

measurementTechnique:
Site description
The study was conducted at the Old Woman Creek (OWC) National Estuarine Research Reserve, located in Huron, Ohio, USA, along the southern shore of Lake Erie. OWC is a natural freshwater estuarine wetland with mineral-rich sediment, characterized by fluctuating water levels and dynamic vegetation. A sand barrier at the estuary's mouth undergoes cycles of buildup and breakdown, periodically isolating the wetland from Lake Erie. The site is part of the AmeriFlux network (US-OWC), measures ecosystem-scale carbon, energy and water fluxes. During the study period, the site experienced significant hydrological and vegetation changes, transitioning from Typha spp. dominance in 2015−2016 to floating-leaved species (Nelumbo spp. and Nymphaea spp.) in 2020−2022.

Flux measurements
Methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) fluxes at the US-OWC AmeriFlux tower (41°22'45.4"N, 82°30'44.4"W) were measured using the eddy covariance method. Sensors were mounted 3 m above the sediment in 2015−2016 and 6 m in 2020−2022. CH4 flux was measured using an LI-7700 analyzer, and CO2 flux was measured with either an LI-7500 (prior to July 30, 2021) or an EC150 (from July 30, 2021 onward), both coupled to a CSAT3 sonic anemometer. Data were logged at 10 Hz using a CR3000 datalogger and averaged over 30-minute periods.

Data post-processing
Half-hourly fluxes were accessed from the AmeriFlux network (Bohrer & Kerns, 2024). Data pre-processing, including flux calculations, was performed as detailed in Rey-Sanchez et al. (2018). Post-processing included:
• Residual spikes removal: Median absolute deviation (MAD) with a z-value of 4 (Papale et al., 2006).
• Friction velocity (USTAR) filtering: CO2 flux (FCO2) measurements during low turbulence periods were filtered using USTAR thresholds determined by the REddyProc package (Wutzler et al., 2018).
• Gap-filling: Half-hourly fluxes were gap-filled separately for two periods (2015−2016 and 2020−2022) using artificial neural networks (ANNs). The gap-filling routine followed the approach described by Knox et al. (2016). Separate models were applied for day and night periods. Daytime FCO2 was gap-filled using variables such as air temperature (TA), photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), wind speed (WS), friction velocity (USTAR), water level, water temperature (TW), the sine (sinWD) and cosine (cosWD) of wind direction, decimal day, and seasonal sine and consine functions. Nighttime FCO2 utilized the same variables, excluding PPFD and VPD. Latent heat flux (LE) was gap-filled using the same variables as daytime FCO2, while methane flux (FCH4) included those variables for daytime FCO2 in addition to LE and atmospheric pressure (PA).
• NEE partitioning: Nighttime FCO2 (observed and gap-filled) was attributed to ecosystem respiration (RE). The best nighttime FCO2 model, trained using ANN on observed data, was used to estimate RE during the day. Gross primary productivity (GPP) was calculated by subtracting NEE from modeled RE (GPP = RE − NEE).
• Uncertainty analysis: The uncertainty procedure follows the approach described in Knox et al. (2019). For random uncertainty, residuals from the median ANN predictions were used to parameterize a Laplace distribution, which was then employed in Monte Carlo simulations to generate 100 realizations of the cumulative fluxes. The variance of these realizations provides an estimate of random uncertainty. For each gap-filled data, gap-filling uncertainty was determined from the variance of 20 ANN predictions. The total uncertainty combines both random and gap-filling uncertainties by adding their variances in quadrature, yielding 95% confidence intervals for the cumulative flux estimates.
